title: See & Spray targeted applications reduce herbicide use while maintaining at least 93% weed control in soybean trials
summary: John Deere's See & Spray machine-vision sprayer gave weed control within 1% of broadcast spraying in soybean trials, with 28.4% early-postemergence and 36.5% mid-postemergence herbicide savings.
account: University of Arkansas weed scientists and Blue River Technology agronomists ran four site-years of randomized complete block trials in 2021 and 2022. Sites were the Northeast Research and Extension Center in Keiser, Arkansas, and Stoneville R&D in Greenville, Mississippi. They compared John Deere See & Spray machine-vision targeted applications with traditional broadcast programs in glyphosate/glufosinate/dicamba-resistant soybean. They used a preemergence residual followed by early-postemergence dicamba and mid-postemergence glufosinate. Targeted applications gave control comparable to broadcast, with at most 1% less efficacy. Overall control was 93% or more for Palmer amaranth, broadleaf signalgrass, morningglory and purslane species. Soybean injury fell by at most 5 percentage points without a yield increase. The results section of the paper assigns mean savings of 62.4% to preemergence, 28.4% to early-postemergence, and 36.5% to mid-postemergence applications, with narrower nozzle angles spraying less area. The paper appeared online on 15 November 2024. The work was a research trial on two research sites, and it reports no commercial farm deployment. Grainews reported on 19 December 2024 that an Iowa State University field-scale trial of See & Spray Ultimate on five fields and 415 acres cut herbicide use by 43.9 to 87.2 percent in 2024, 76 percent on average. In a three-year study published on 4 November 2025 and funded by Blue River, the same Arkansas group found no seedbank increase at the highest sensitivity. At the lowest sensitivity, weed density rose from 867 to 11,300 plants per hectare. On the same day John Deere reported that customers ran See & Spray on more than five million acres in the 2025 season, cutting non-residual herbicide use by nearly half.
purpose: Detect weeds with machine vision and apply herbicide only where weeds are present, reducing herbicide use while maintaining control.
system: John Deere See & Spray (machine-vision targeted sprayer)
model_version: See & Spray model year 2022 (level 3 detection sensitivity, small coverage buffer)
deployer: University of Arkansas and Stoneville R&D field trials (Keiser, AR and Greenville, MS)
taxonomy_note: Herbicide saved is read as reduced waste; it is also a cost saving for the grower.

ratings.reason: The researchers measured mean herbicide savings of 28.4% to 62.4% across the three application timings, with weed control comparable to broadcast spraying and no yield increase. These savings lower the grower's input costs.
Less herbicide was sprayed in the trials, but no source reports a measured environmental outcome off the plots.

ai_role.statement: The machine-vision sprayer decided where to spray, and the randomized trial held herbicides and rates constant, so the savings come from targeting. Savings depended on nozzle angle and the sensitivity setting chosen by the operator. A three-year follow-up by the same group found no seedbank increase at the highest sensitivity, while at the lowest setting weed density rose, which the authors attribute to Palmer amaranth escapes. The maker's agronomists co-wrote the trial paper, and the maker funded both studies.

fields.account: University of Arkansas weed scientists and Blue River Technology agronomists ran four site-years of randomized complete block trials in 2021 and 2022. Sites were the Northeast Research and Extension Center in Keiser, Arkansas, and Stoneville R&D in Greenville, Mississippi.
